name: front-controller
intent: Consolidate all request handling behind a single entry point that performs the shared cross-cutting processing - authentication, session and locale resolution, logging, error mapping - exactly once for every request and then dispatches to a request-specific handler.
problem: Every request must pass through the same preliminary work (authentication/authorization, session and locale resolution, logging/tracing, encoding, error mapping) before any request-specific logic runs. When each page or endpoint invokes those services itself, the behaviour drifts between endpoints, new handlers silently omit security checks, navigation and error handling are duplicated in many places, and changing how requests are dispatched means editing every entry point.
context: Server-side presentation layers and HTTP APIs where many endpoints share a lifecycle: a common set of checks applies to all requests, requests must be routed to request-specific handlers, and responses must be mapped to representations consistently. It applies to classic server-rendered web applications and to modern API services alike; because nearly every web framework is built around this pattern, the live decision is usually how to structure and order the framework's single entry point rather than whether to have one.
benefits: Shared behaviour is implemented once and applied to every request: authentication/authorization, session handling, logging, internationalization and error mapping cannot be forgotten by a newly added endpoint.
Views and handlers are freed from control logic - one point of control and dispatch means navigation, preconditions and content selection are not duplicated across pages.
Security improves structurally: a single, auditable enforcement point for authentication, CSRF protection and rate limiting instead of per-endpoint checks that erode over time.
Routing is declarative and extensible: new endpoints register with the dispatcher and new cross-cutting concerns arrive as an added stage, without editing existing handlers.
Consistent observability and error handling: one place assigns request ids, measures the whole pipeline and maps exceptions to responses, so failures look the same everywhere.
The dispatch table and the middleware chain are unit-testable independently of the endpoint logic, and a handler can be exercised behind the same chain it meets in production.
tradeoffs: The dispatch and middleware layer is an indirection: control flow is assembled at startup, so understanding why a request got a particular response means reading routing and filter configuration, not just the handler.
Blast radius: every request shares one chain, so a slow stage, a misordered filter or a bug in the front controller affects all endpoints at once.

Ordering requirements are implicit: authentication must precede authorization, session resolution must precede authentication, error mapping must be outermost, and body parsing must precede handlers - these dependencies are expressed only by registration order and are invisible at the call site.

The controller is a gravity well: because it is the one obvious place to add a check, request-specific business logic accumulates there until it degenerates into an Application Controller or god object.
Framework lock-in and migration cost: once every request enters through the framework's controller, replacing that framework means rewriting routing, filters and the entry point together.

An extra dispatch hop and per-request context allocation are paid on every request, and a stateful controller or middleware serializes traffic - the entry point must stay stateless to keep the performance cost bounded.

participants.responsibility: Single entry point invoked for every request; runs the shared behaviour (auth, session, logging, error mapping) and hands the request to the dispatcher without containing request-specific logic.
Selects the request-specific handler or command from method/path (route table, registry, router); may be embedded in the controller or a separate component.
Encapsulates the behaviour of one kind of request and contains the business logic the front controller must not hold; produces a result or a view name.
Renders the response representation from the model produced by the handler, without control logic of its own.
Prepares or adapts data for the view (view-model assembly, formatting, content selection) so the view and the controller both stay free of presentation logic.

use_cases: Web applications that must enforce authentication, session handling and CSRF checks uniformly before any page or controller runs.
HTTP APIs where versioning, content negotiation, rate limiting and request-id propagation apply to every route.
Multi-channel or multi-tenant systems where locale and tenant resolution plus error mapping must be identical across all endpoints.
Framework and platform code that offers a single plug-in point (middleware, filters, interceptors, plugins) for application teams to extend.
Applications whose routing must be changeable centrally: feature flags, redirect maps, gradual migrations and A/B splits of endpoints.

Enterprise applications where multiple teams contribute endpoints over time and require uniform security policy enforcement, consistent logging formats, and a single control point for rate limiting and feature flags.
E-commerce checkout, onboarding wizard, or approval flows where a complex multi-step process spans several HTTP requests and screen navigation must be coordinated from a single controller.

Microservices API gateway: all incoming traffic enters through a gateway front controller that handles auth token validation, rate limiting, request routing and response transformation before forwarding to downstream services.

Multi-tenant SaaS platform: tenant resolution, feature-flag evaluation and tenant-scoped configuration injection happen in the front controller so all downstream business logic runs in the correct tenant context.
Progressive Web App (PWA) backend: service-worker registration, cache-policy enforcement and offline-first data synchronization are coordinated from the front controller for all API routes.
GraphQL server with unified error handling: the front controller normalises GraphQL errors to a consistent error-response shape, enforces query complexity limits and applies auth at the entry point.

Legacy system wrapping: a modern front controller proxies or redirects requests into a legacy system, hiding the legacy URL structure and normalising authentication and session schemes across both systems.

Spring MVC: the Spring Framework's DispatcherServlet is an explicit front controller: one central servlet provides the shared request-processing algorithm while delegate components handle mapping, view resolution and exception handling.

ASP.NET Core: a WebApplication request-delegate pipeline can serve as the front-controller boundary, with Use/Map/Run stages applying shared work and selecting terminal handlers; the documented order and short-circuit rules must remain explicit.

Django: the MIDDLEWARE setting builds one request/response chain around views, making global security, session and response hooks consistent while requiring declared ordering (AuthenticationMiddleware depends on SessionMiddleware).
avoid_when: A single-endpoint service, health probe or batch tool: one handler function is the whole application and the dispatch layer adds nothing.
The framework already owns the entry point (Spring MVC, ASP.NET Core, Ktor, Rails, Vapor, axum, Express): register into that pipeline instead of building a second front controller inside it.
The real decision is how one workflow spans several requests - that is an Application Controller, not a front controller.
Only one cross-cutting concern exists and it can be attached to the affected paths with a single decorator, Intercepting Filter or gateway policy.
anti_patterns: God controller: request handling and business logic migrate into the front controller until it is the application, defeating the separation the pattern exists for.
Building a second dispatcher inside a framework that already provides one: custom route matching or duplicate authentication checks in front of the framework router.
Long if/else chains over the URL instead of a route table or command registry, so every new endpoint edits the controller and re-tests everything.
Middleware that swallows exceptions or redirects silently, hiding 404/500 semantics and making failures invisible to monitoring.
Per-request mutable state on the controller or middleware instance that frameworks instantiate once and share across concurrent requests.

Middleware ordering violations: authentication middleware registered after protected routes, or session resolution running before authentication has resolved the principal, silently bypassing the very checks the chain was designed to enforce.

Response state corruption: writing headers or status codes after the response has started being sent, causing 'headers already sent' exceptions; the front controller must ensure error handlers can still run even when a response is partially written.
God middleware: one middleware handling auth, logging, CORS, rate-limiting and body parsing together, making ordering impossible to reason about and failures in one concern breaking all others.

Middleware that conditionally short-circuits based on path (e.g. skipping auth for /health) without an explicit allowlist; this silently creates unauthenticated routes that are invisible in the route table.
Registering a stage that mutates the request object after another stage has already read and cached values from it, producing inconsistent behaviour depending on registration order.
Returning a response directly from a middleware stage instead of passing control to the next stage, preventing downstream stages (e.g. audit logging, metrics) from running.
Storing sensitive data (tokens, tenant IDs) in mutable front-controller instance fields instead of a request-scoped context object, risking data leakage between concurrent requests.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: shared request processing (dispatch, authentication, logging) versus request-specific behaviour.
Single Responsibility: the controller dispatches; commands and handlers contain the logic; views render.
DRY: cross-cutting behaviour is implemented once for all requests instead of per endpoint.
Open/Closed: new endpoints arrive by registration and new cross-cutting concerns by adding a stage, without editing existing handlers.
Keep the entry point thin and depend on abstract handler contracts so the dispatcher does not know concrete pages.
best_practices: Keep the front controller thin: dispatch plus the shared chain; anything request-specific belongs in a handler or command.
Make the chain explicit and ordered at startup (a list, registry or builder) and document which stages may short-circuit a request.
Use a declarative route table or registry rather than conditionals in code.
Centralize error-to-response mapping and request correlation so every endpoint reports failures identically.
Keep the controller and all middleware stateless; per-request state belongs in a request/context object or the request itself.
Treat the entry point as a security boundary: default-deny, audit it, and verify that newly registered routes cannot bypass the shared authentication stage.

Register middleware in the correct order: guard middleware (authentication, rate-limiting, CSRF) must execute before the routes they protect, never after; document ordering dependencies explicitly in the pipeline definition.

Implement single-responsibility middleware: split combined middleware (auth + logging + CORS + rate-limiting) into focused, named components; avoids the god-middleware anti-pattern and makes ordering violations obvious.

Measure and profile the pipeline: each stage adds microseconds of latency; a chain of more than 20 middleware in hot request paths can measurably degrade p99 latency; profile before and after adding stages.

Apply the pipeline consistently across all environments (dev, staging, prod): a front controller that behaves differently in dev vs. prod creates invisible production-only bugs; test the full chain in integration tests.
Design stages to be idempotent and commutative where possible: a logging or metrics stage should be safe to run on retry; a session-resolution stage should be safe to call twice.

Use structured request-correlation IDs (e.g. OpenTelemetry trace-id, X-Request-ID header) injected at the front controller and propagated through the entire chain so that logs can be assembled per-request across all stages.
Set per-stage timeouts and fail-open or fail-closed appropriately: an authentication stage that times out should fail closed (deny), while a metrics stage should fail open (continue).
Make pipeline composition explicit in code (a sorted list, a builder DSL, or a config file) rather than implicit in registration order; treat the pipeline definition as a first-class artifact.
Version the pipeline: treat breaking changes to stage order or short-circuit semantics as a breaking API change, and gate them behind feature flags or API version prefixes.
Instrument each stage individually with metrics (histogram of latency, counter of short-circuits) so that a slow stage can be identified without decomposing the whole request trace.

When integrating with an existing framework entry point (e.g. DispatcherServlet, Ktor, Express), do not build a second parallel front controller; instead register your concerns as middleware or filters into the framework's own pipeline.
For multi-tenant SaaS or API gateways, resolve tenant context (schema, config, feature flags) as the very first stage so that all downstream stages and handlers operate on a tenant-isolated context.
Implement graceful shutdown: the front controller should drain in-flight requests before stopping so that a deployment does not abort requests mid-processing.
